page_title_verbatim: Automating Classic Market Methods in MQL5 (Part 9): Linda Bradford Raschke's 3/10 Oscillator System
author: Go to Freelance
name: Linda Bradford Raschke 3/10 Oscillator ('Anti') & 20-EMA ADX ('Holy Grail') Swing Pullback
economic_rationale: Strong directional trends (ADX > 30) rarely reverse on the first retracement; entering the first pullback to the 20-EMA or 3/10 oscillator hook captures institutional trend continuation with tight structural invalidation.
counterparty_mechanism: Early profit-taking creates a temporary counter-trend retracement to the 20-EMA while institutional trend flows remain active, forcing late shorts/longs to cover on trend resumption.
entry_rule: Two H1/H4 swing pullback setups: (1) Anti: SMA(3)-SMA(10) oscillator with 16-SMA signal line enters on first oscillator pullback after signal crosses zero with price confirmation; (2) Holy Grail: ADX(14) > 30 and rising, enter on first price pullback touching EMA(20) in trend direction.
exit_rule: Anti exits when fast 3/10 line crosses back through the 16-SMA signal line against the trade; Holy Grail exits when ADX(14) drops below 20 signaling trend termination.
stop_loss_rule: Hard structural stop loss placed at the pullback swing extreme, with optional ATR buffer (InpATRStopMult > 0).
take_profit_rule: Dynamic exit on opposite 3/10 signal-line cross (Anti) or ADX(14) < 20 trend exhaustion (Holy Grail).
rule_description: White-box MQL5 automation of Linda Bradford Raschke's H1/H4 swing pullback systems: Anti (3/10/16 oscillator first pullback post-zero cross) and Holy Grail (ADX(14)>30 rising trend first pullback to EMA(20)), with swing-extreme hard stop (+ optional ATR buffer) and signal-cross / ADX<20 exits. Zero grid, zero martingale.

raw_text: MetaTrader 5 — Examples | 22 October [REDACTED_PERIOD], 10:18 1 677 0 Tola Moses Hector Introduction Linda Bradford Raschke began trading futures on the floor in 1981, moved to screen trading in the mid-1980s, and published "Street Smarts" with Larry Connors in 1996. She has traded her own account continuously since then. The methods in that book—particularly the 3/10 oscillator and the holy grail setup—have remained in active use among short-term swing traders for nearly thirty years. Raschke's methods differ from the systems in Parts 5–8 in timeframe and required precision. Those systems— Turtle rules , Livermore's market key , Darvas boxes , and Seykota's EMA system —operate on daily or weekly bars and require patience measured in weeks. Raschke's methods operate on H1 or H4 bars and require precision measured in sessions. Signals are more frequent, stops are tighter, and exits are more specific. This article automates two of her setups: the "Anti," which enters on the first oscillator pullback after a trend change confirmed by the signal line crossing zero; and the "Holy Grail," which enters on the first price pullback to the 20-period EMA in a strong, rising ADX trend. Fig. 1. System demonstration. This EA answers two questions: Does the 3/10 oscillator confirm a trend change and then trigger an Anti entry with price confirmation? Is ADX above 30 and rising for at least two bars, with price pulling back to the 20‑period EMA for a first‑pullback entry? We will cover the following topics: The 3/10 Oscillator—Construction and Interpretation The Anti Setup—Theory and Rules The Holy Grail Setup—Theory and Rules Architecture—Two State Machines, One EA Implementation in MQL5 Known Limitations and Design Decisions Conclusion The 3/10 Oscillator—Construction and Interpretation Raschke described the 3/10 oscillator as a tool she had used since 1981. It is a MACD variant with different periods and a critical construction difference: it uses simple moving averages throughout, not exponential ones. The fast line is SMA(fast) minus SMA(slow) of closing prices—3 and 10 periods by default. This difference oscillates around zero and captures short-term momentum. The signal line is SMA(signal) of the fast line—16 periods by default. It is slower and smoother. When the fast line is above the signal line, short-term momentum is bullish. When it is below, momentum is bearish. The signal line crossing zero is the trend change confirmation. When the signal line crosses from below zero to above, the overall momentum has shifted bullish. When it crosses from above to below, it has shifted bearish. This 3/10/16 construction produces faster cycles than the standard MACD (12, 26, 9) and is tuned specifically for swing trading on hourly (H1) and 4-hour (H4) bars. On a standard MACD, the signal line zero cross on H1 data may lag the actual price move by many bars. On the 3/10 oscillator, the lag is substantially reduced. In MQL5, the 3/10 oscillator is computed manually from price arrays because the signal line is an SMA of the fast line—not a native MetaTrader indicator type. This article calculates both lines from price arrays on each bar, avoiding additional file dependencies. The Anti Setup—Theory and Rules The "Anti" is Raschke's own name for the setup. It enters against the most recent short-term direction—buying a pullback during a newly confirmed bullish trend, or selling a rally during a newly confirmed bearish trend. The conditions are sequential, and all must be satisfied in order. Step 1—Signal line zero cross : the 16-period signal line crosses from below to above zero (bullish confirmation) or from above to below zero (bearish confirmation). This does not trigger an entry; it opens a window for one. Step 2—Fast line pullback : after the zero cross, the fast line moves against the new trend direction until it touches or crosses the signal line. For a bullish confirmation, the fast line dips to at or below the signal line. This is the slingshot loading phase. This EA requires the fast line to touch or cross the signal line—approaches that do not reach it are not counted as valid pullbacks. Step 3—Fast line reversal cross : the fast line crosses back through the signal line in the direction of the new trend (above, for bull Anti). This is the trigger. Note: if this cross occurs but price confirmation fails (Step 4), the window closes entirely. The EA does not wait for a second cross—only the first reversal cross after a valid pullback qualifies. Step 4—Price confirmation : the most recently closed bar must have closed in the direction of the new trend. For a bull Anti, the close must be higher than the previous bar's close. For a bear Anti, it must be lower. Step 5—Entry : on the first tick of the next bar, using a market order. The EA enters at the then-current Ask (buy) or Bid (sell), which may differ slightly from the bar’s open price. Stop: at the pullback extreme. For a bullish Anti, use the lowest low of the pullback; for a bearish Anti, use the highest high. An ATR buffer can be added via input parameter (default: zero). Exit: when the fast line crosses back through the signal line in the direction opposite to the trade. The Holy Grail Setup—Theory and Rules The "Holy Grail" requires a genuine, strengthening trend—not just a trend, but a trend gaining momentum—and enters at the moment where price offers its lowest-risk pullback point within that trend. Step 1—Strong trend : ADX must be at or above 30 and must have been rising for at least two consecutive bars (ADX current > ADX previous > ADX two bars ago). Above 30 alone is not sufficient; the trend must be actively strengthening. Step 2—EMA direction : the 20-period EMA must be sloping in the direction of the intended trade. Direction is determined by comparing the current bar's EMA value to the previous bar's value. One bar of EMA slope is admittedly a noisy signal; the ADX condition in Step 1 is the primary trend-quality filter. Step 3—Pullback to EMA : the price must pull back to touch the 20-period EMA. For a long, the bar's low must be at or below the EMA. For a short, the bar's high must be at or above the EMA. Step 4—First pullback only : only the first qualifying pullback after an ADX confirmation is taken. A second entry is allowed only after ADX drops below 30 and later returns above 30 with two consecutive rising bars. This reset is tracked explicitly in state; the EA does not allow re-entry simply because the prior trade closed. Step 5—Entry : on the first tick of the next bar after the pullback bar, using a market order at the then-current Ask (buy) or Bid (sell), which may differ slightly from the bar’s open price. Stop: at the extreme of the pullback bar—the low of the bar for longs, the high for shorts. An ATR buffer can be added via an input parameter (default: zero). Exit 1: when ADX drops below 20—the trend is considered ended. Exit 2: when the closing price crosses the 20-period EMA in the direction against the trade. Architecture—Two State Machines, One EA Both setups run as independent state machines in a single EA called "RaschkeEA.mq5." On each new bar, the EA runs both state machines. Either can generate a trade; however, only one position is open at a time. The two state machines maintain separate direction variables. The "g_anti_is_long" stores the "Anti's" direction; "g_hg_is_long" stores the "Holy Grail's" direction. Using a single shared direction variable would create the risk that one state machine's direction assignment overwrites the other's while the latter is in a waiting state. Processing order : when both setups are enabled and no position is open, one must be evaluated first. By default, the "Anti" is processed first. If both setups simultaneously reach their entry condition on the same bar, the Anti takes priority. This behavior is configurable via "InpAntiFirst" and is disclosed in the log.
